ScoringBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Tabular Foundation Models with Proper Scoring Rules

Jonas Landsgesell ††thanks: jonaslandsgesell_at_gmail dot com Affiliation: University of Stuttgart (Stuttgart, Germany)    Pascal Knoll ††thanks: knollpascal00_at_gmail dot com Affiliation: University of Stuttgart (Stuttgart, Germany)    Tizian Wenzel ††thanks: wenzel_at_math dot lmu dot de Affiliation: Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (Munich, Germany) Affiliation: Munich Center for Machine Learning (Munich, Germany)
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN (Hollmann et al., 2025) and TabICL (Qu et al., 2026) already produce full predictive distributions, yet prevailing regression benchmarks evaluate them almost exclusively via point-estimate metrics (RMSE, R2R^{2}). This discards precisely the distributional information these models are designed to provide — a critical gap for high-stakes domains where not all kinds of errors are equally costly.

We introduce ScoringBench11 1 ScoringBench is available at https://github.com/jonaslandsgesell/ScoringBench., an open and extensible benchmark that evaluates tabular regression models under a comprehensive suite of proper scoring rules — including CRPS, CRLS, interval score, energy score, and weighted CRPS — alongside standard point metrics. ScoringBench covers 97 regression datasets from diverse domains, supports transparent community contributions via a git-based leaderboard, and provides two complementary ranking protocols: an ordinal Demšar/autorank approach and a magnitude-preserving z-score ranking approach.

Evaluating several models — spanning in-context learners, fine-tuned foundation models, gradient-boosted trees, and MLPs — we find that model rankings shift substantially depending on the scoring rule: models that excel on point-estimate metrics can rank poorly on probabilistic ones, and the top-performing model under one proper scoring rule may rank noticeably lower under another. These results demonstrate that the choice of evaluation metric is not a technicality but a modelling decision — and, for applications where e.g. tail errors are disproportionately costly, a domain-specific requirement with direct consequences for model deployment.

1 Introduction

The emergence of Prior-Data Fitted Networks (TabPFN) (Hollmann et al., 2022; Hollmann et al., 2025) has shifted tabular learning towards in-context learners (Qu et al., 2026) that place attention on informative examples at inference time without model weight updates. Both leading models (TabPFN and TabICLv2) perform discretized distributional regression and produce full predictive distributions: TabPFN predicts a probability mass function over an adaptive grid, while TabICLv2 performs multi-quantile regression (approximating the CRPS training objective with a limited number of quantiles).

Despite this, prevailing tabular benchmarks (TabArena (Erickson et al., 2025), TALENT (Liu et al., 2025)) evaluate models almost exclusively through point-estimate metrics such as RMSE or R2R^{2}, implicitly rewarding models that elicit a good conditional mean while ignoring the quality of the full predictive distribution. This evaluation mismatch is not merely cosmetic. Gneiting and Raftery (2007) proposed to use optimal score estimation as a general framework for estimation. A scoring rule S⁡(F,y)S(F,y) measures the quality of a probabilistic forecast FF when a realization yy is observed and is strictly proper if the expected scoring rule is minimized if and only if the forecast FF equals the true distribution.

Since a scoring rule encodes how to penalize specific deviations, there exist infinitely many proper scoring rules: we summarize and argue that different rules induce different inductive biases during finite-sample training, even though they share the same population minimizer (Landsgesell and Knoll, 2026; Waghmare and Ziegel, 2025; Buchweitz et al., 2025). Consequently, different proper scoring rules yield different model rankings (Merkle and Steyvers, 2013; Landsgesell and Knoll, 2026). For point estimation, Gneiting (2011) argues that “the common practice of requesting some point forecast, and then evaluating the forecasters by using some (set of) scoring function(s), is not a meaningful endeavor.” Instead, effective forecasting requires clear directives, such as disclosing the evaluation metric ex ante. The same argument applies to distributional regression: requesting a predictive distribution but not disclosing the scoring rule for evaluation risks weighting errors suboptimally for the undisclosed scoring rule (e.g. it is unclear if tail accuracy or central tendency shall be rewarded), especially in the finite-sample regime.

We show this inductive bias stemming from the choice of scoring rule in the context of tabular distributional regression setting in Landsgesell and Knoll (2026):

θ1=arg⁡minθ​𝔼^(Xi,Yi)i=1n​[S⁡(Fθ​(Xi),Yi)],θ2=arg⁡minθ​𝔼^(Xi,Yi)i=1n​[S′​(Fθ​(Xi),Yi)]⇏Fθ1=Fθ2.\displaystyle\theta_{1}=\arg\min_{\theta}\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{(X_{i},Y_{i})_{i=1}^{n}}[S(F_{\theta}(X_{i}),Y_{i})],\quad\theta_{2}=\arg\min_{\theta}\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{(X_{i},Y_{i})_{i=1}^{n}}[S^{\prime}(F_{\theta}(X_{i}),Y_{i})]\nRightarrow F_{\theta_{1}}=F_{\theta_{2}}.

Here, θ1\theta_{1} and θ2\theta_{2} are the parameter values obtained by minimizing the two scoring rules SS and S′S^{\prime}; Fθ​(Xi)F_{\theta}(X_{i}) denotes the model’s predictive distribution at input XiX_{i}, YiY_{i} is the observed outcome, and 𝔼^(Xi,Yi)i=1n\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{(X_{i},Y_{i})_{i=1}^{n}} is the sample average 1n​∑i=1n(⋅)\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\cdot). The symbol ⇏\nRightarrow indicates that, in finite samples, different empirical scoring rules can yield different fitted predictive mappings even when the scoring rules share the same population minimizer.

The difference in inductive bias is not just a theoretical curiosity but has practical implications for model selection and deployment which is why we argue that benchmarks should report a comprehensive suite of proper scoring rules alongside standard point metrics — even if high-risk applications may require custom proper scoring rules that encode the desired error penalties (Oesterheld and Conitzer, 2020; Johnstone et al., 2011).

ScoringBench implements these ideas in an extensible, reproducible evaluation harness covering a broad set of scoring rules. Our fine-tuning experiments with custom losses show that high-risk applications—where different errors have different impacts can benefit from pretraining or fine-tuning with a scoring rule that encodes the desired error penalties. Relying only on point-estimate metrics can hide these important differences. Even when the focus is on mean estimators, Bregman divergences can help induce desired residual structures (Gneiting, 2011). Some high-risk settings require carefully designed custom proper scoring rules (Oesterheld and Conitzer, 2020; Johnstone et al., 2011). This view aligns with the seminal works of Gneiting and Raftery (2007); Gneiting (2011); Gneiting and Ranjan (2011).

1.1 Contributions

We contribute

  • •

    ScoringBench (https://github.com/jonaslandsgesell/ScoringBench), an easy-to-install benchmark for distributional regression with minimal dependencies.

  • •

    a git-based leaderboard (https://scoringbench.com/), where updates happen transparently with full traceability and reproducibility.

  • •

    a rigorous benchmark protocol using Autorank (following Demšar (2006); Herbold (2020)).

2 Related Work

Tabular Deep Learning.

Prior-Data Fitted Networks (TabPFN) (Hollmann et al., 2022; Hollmann et al., 2025) have shifted tabular learning from the dominant paradigm of gradient-boosted decision trees toward transformer-based in-context learners. Rather than updating model weights at training time, TabPFN performs in-context learning in a single forward pass, naturally producing a full predictive distribution over an adaptive output grid. TabICLv2 (Qu et al., 2026) performs many conditional quantile regressions, yielding a distributional output, coupled to in-context learning. Both architectures are therefore inherently probabilistic: they predict probability mass functions (or dense quantile functions) rather than single point estimates. Despite this capability, prevailing evaluations of these models (Erickson et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025) still rely almost exclusively on point-estimate metrics, effectively discarding the distributional information these architectures are designed to provide. ScoringBench is designed to close this evaluation gap.

Probabilistic Forecasting.

The theoretical foundations for evaluating probabilistic predictions were laid by Gneiting and Raftery (2007), who characterized the space of strictly proper scoring rules—scoring rules S⁡(F,y)S(F,y) for which the expected score is uniquely minimized when the forecast FF equals the true data-generating distribution. Gneiting et al. (2007) further formalized the goal of probabilistic forecasting as maximizing sharpness subject to calibration, providing the conceptual basis for the diagnostics reported in ScoringBench. Importantly, while all strictly proper scoring rules share the same population-level minimizer, they induce different inductive biases during finite-sample training (Waghmare and Ziegel, 2025). Merkle and Steyvers (2013) demonstrated empirically that model rankings change substantially depending on which proper scoring rule is used (the Spearman correlation between Brier-score and log-score rankings in their study is only 0.150.15), and Buchweitz et al. (2025) showed that a broad class of proper scoring rules—including the logarithmic, CRPS, quadratic, and energy scores—penalize under- and overestimation asymmetrically. The scoring rules computed in ScoringBench span a wide range of sensitivities: the CRPS (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007) weights all quantile levels equally; the energy score (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007) generalizes CRPS via the parameter β∈(0,2)\beta\in(0,2), interpolating between median- and mean-optimal behavior (Landsgesell and Knoll, 2026); the interval score (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007) targets specific central prediction intervals; and the weighted CRPS (Gneiting and Ranjan, 2011) allows practitioners to emphasize particular regions of the predictive distribution. Together, these rules enable a multifaceted assessment of forecast quality that no single metric can provide.

Benchmarking Methodology.

Two prominent tabular benchmarks, TabArena (Erickson et al., 2025) and TALENT (Liu et al., 2025), evaluate models exclusively on point-estimate metrics such as RMSE and R2R^{2}. These metrics reward accurate conditional-mean predictions but are blind to the quality of the full predictive distribution. As Gneiting (2011) argues, requesting some point forecast and then evaluating it with some scoring function “is not a meaningful endeavor”; effective evaluation requires either disclosing the scoring function ex ante or requesting a specific functional of the forecaster’s predictive distribution. Landsgesell and Knoll (2026) extended this argument to the tabular distributional regression setting, showing that fine-tuning realTabPFNv2.5 Garg et al. (2025); Grinsztajn et al. (2025) with a scoring rule different from the pretraining objective shifts the model’s inductive bias and changes its ranking across benchmark datasets. Other recent work, including Izbicki and Rodrigues (2026), has similarly highlighted the limitations of relying solely on point-estimate metrics; Izbicki et al. propose an additional loss termed “conditional density estimation”, which can be viewed as a Brier-type loss for continuous outcomes (Rudemo, 1982). Building on our preprint (Landsgesell and Knoll, 2026), ScoringBench offers a broad framework in which any proper scoring rule can be used for evaluation; by reporting a comprehensive suite of such rules, the benchmark helps account for the distinct finite-sample inductive biases induced by different scoring choices and establishes a reproducible, unified evaluation protocol for distributional regression.

3 ScoringBench Setup

3.1 Benchmarking with Proper Scoring Rules

We refer the reader to Gneiting and Raftery (2007); Gneiting and Ranjan (2011) for a comprehensive introduction to proper scoring rules and Landsgesell and Knoll (2026) for a discussion in the tabular distributional regression setting. ScoringBench computes a compact suite of proper scoring rules (CRPS, CRLS, interval score, β\beta-energy score, weighted CRPS, log score, the CDE loss and others) alongside standard point metrics. All definitions follow Gneiting and Raftery (2007); Gneiting and Ranjan (2011) unless otherwise noted; definitions and formulae are provided in the Appendix A.1 and Appendix A.2.

3.2 Datasets

Many existing tabular benchmarks assemble datasets via semi-automated pipelines (Gijsbers et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2026; Grinsztajn et al., 2022) or manual curation (Erickson et al., 2025; Grinsztajn et al., 2022). Building on these efforts, ScoringBench curates a heterogeneous collection of regression problems spanning finance, physics, engineering, and environmental science, and evaluates them under a suite of proper scoring rules that go beyond point-estimate metrics to assess calibration, sharpness, and tail behavior (e.g., the interval score jointly penalizes over-wide intervals and coverage shortfalls).

Our dataset collection incorporates the three OpenML regression suites 269, 297, and 299 (Dheur and Taieb, 2023). To increase the number of datasets, we supplement these suites with datasets. The supplements are drawn from three additional repositories: PMLB (Olson et al., 2017), KEEL (Derrac et al., 2015), and TALENT (Liu et al., 2025). We drop duplicated datasets by filtering the names and also drop datasets that have only two unique target values (binary classification, not regression). Lightweight, uniform preprocessing is applied (numeric median imputation, categorical mode imputation, and label-encoding); see Appendix B.3 for details on the imputation and preprocessing pipeline. The complete list of datasets retained after deduplication and validation, together with per-dataset details and selection criteria, is provided in Appendix B.

For each dataset, models (see Section 3.3) are evaluated using 55-fold cross-validation with a fixed random seed. We limit each training fold to at most 2400 observations and each test fold to at most 600 observations.

3.3 Evaluated Models

We evaluate a mix of in-context learners and conventional, non-pretrained baselines. The in-context models comprise realTabPFNv2.5 (the baseline TabPFN variant used for fine-tuning), several fine-tuned variants of realTabPFNv2.5 trained with different scoring-rule objectives, TabPFNv2.6 (a newer TabPFN release), and TabICLv2, a transformer-based in-context learner that estimates multiple quantiles. As non-pretrained baselines we include XGBoost vector-leaf models adapted for distributional regression, XGBoostLLS (März, 2019), CatBoost (Prokhorenkova et al., 2018) and CREPES (Boström, 2024) for conformal predictive distributions on top of XGBoost and CatBoost or TabICLv2. We also evaluate TabM (Gorishniy et al., 2024), a compact multilayer perceptron that leverages parameter-efficient ensembling, and RealMLP (Holzmüller et al., 2024), an MLP architecture with extensive hyperparameter tuning designed for robust out-of-the-box performance on diverse tabular tasks.

3.4 Ranking

We use two complementary ranking strategies; full details are in Appendix D. The benchmark produces scores sm,d,f,ps_{m,d,f,p} for each tuple

(model ​m,dataset ​d,fold ​f,metric ​p),\displaystyle(\text{model }m,\penalty\ \text{dataset }d,\penalty\ \text{fold }f,\penalty\ \text{metric }p),

across MM models, DD datasets, FF folds, and PP metrics (in total M⋅D⋅F⋅PM\cdot D\cdot F\cdot P observations). Before ranking, we collapse across folds by averaging,

s¯m,d,p=1F​∑f=1Fsm,d,f,p,\displaystyle\bar{s}_{m,d,p}\;=\;\frac{1}{F}\sum_{f=1}^{F}s_{m,d,f,p}\,,

reducing the data to per-(model, dataset, metric) scores. This step is essential to avoid pseudoreplication: fold-level scores within a dataset are correlated, so treating them as independent observations would inflate the effective sample size and distort subsequent tests (Lazic, 2010). Following Lazic (2010), each dataset acts as an experimental subject and its folds as repeated measurements — these must be collapsed before any cross-dataset comparison. The two ranking strategies then differ in how they aggregate these per-dataset summaries s¯m,d,p\bar{s}_{m,d,p} across datasets:

After fold aggregation the data has shape M×D×PM\times D\times P, with entries s¯m,d,p\bar{s}_{m,d,p} denoting the fold-averaged score of model mm on dataset dd for metric pp. The two ranking strategies differ in how they aggregate these per-dataset summaries across datasets:

Demšar–autorank approach (Autorank).

Following Demšar (Demšar, 2006) and the autorank library (Herbold, 2020), models are ranked within each dataset (best = rank 0), mean ranks are computed across datasets, and a non-parametric Friedman omnibus test evaluates whether mean ranks differ across models. If the omnibus test is significant, Nemenyi post-hoc comparisons (visualized via a critical-difference diagram) identify which model pairs differ; we also report Akinshin’s γ\gamma as a non-parametric analogue of Cohen’s dd 22 2 https://aakinshin.net/posts/nonparametric-effect-size/. Thresholds on Akinshin’s γ\gamma used to categorize effect sizes in the Autorank library follow the common practice for Cohen’s d: γ<0.2\gamma<0.2 is negligible; 0.2≤γ<0.50.2\leq\gamma<0.5 is small; 0.5≤γ<0.80.5\leq\gamma<0.8 is medium; γ≥0.8\gamma\geq 0.8 is large. This ordinal approach is robust to outliers and to heteroskedastic score scales, but it discards magnitude information by relying on ranks. Some more details are provided in Section D.1. See the Autorank-based heatmap in Figure 2(a).

Per-dataset standardized performance approach (z-score ranking).

To preserve magnitude information while controlling for dataset difficulty, we standardize the fold-averaged scores within each dataset (compute zz-scores across the MM models, negating the sign for metrics where smaller is better), then average these standardized scores across datasets and rank models by their mean standardized performance. The full details are given in Section D.2. This produces magnitude-preserving, comparable scores across datasets that account for differing score scales and difficulties. See the effect-size heatmap in Figure 2(b).

We refer to the Demšar–autorank procedure as Autorank and the per-dataset standardized performance procedure as z-score ranking; subsequent figures and tables use these labels. The two approaches are complementary (ordinal significance vs. magnitude-aware ranking); for implementation details see Appendix D. Since both produce highly correlated rankings across metrics (mean Pearson r≈0.90r\approx 0.90; see Section D.3), we report only the Autorank-based leaderboards in the main text. Full z-score rankings and per-metric correlation statistics are available on the live leaderboard.

4 Results of Benchmark 2026

Our website

https://scoringbench.com/

reports the live leaderboard. Hyperparameters of the models are documented in the repository. The leaderboard is updated with every new pull request, and all changes are tracked in the git history for full reproducibility, transparency and agility.

Our results confirm the central finding of Landsgesell and Knoll (2026): the choice of scoring rule for fine-tuning and pretraining shapes model behavior beyond what population-level propriety guarantees, and reporting only point-estimate metrics risks obscuring these differences.

Table 1 reports Autorank-based rankings for CRPS (lower is better); column headers are defined in the table caption. Several fine-tuned TabPFN variants dominate the ordering: the top-ranked model is finetune_tabpfn_realv2_5_crls (mean rank ≈8.55\approx 8.55), with median CRPS around 0.390.39 for the leading cluster versus up to ∼0.55{\sim}0.55 for gradient-boosted baselines, indicating meaningful differences in probabilistic calibration and sharpness. While Akinshin’s γ\gamma values remain in the “negligible” range throughout, the rank ordering is consistent across datasets and robust to dataset size (see Appendix E), suggesting that fine-tuning induces subtle but stable shifts in predictive behavior. Thresholds on Akinshin’s γ\gamma used to categorize effect sizes in the Autorank library follow the common practice for Cohen’s d according to Romano et al. (2006): γ<0.2\gamma<0.2 is negligible; 0.2≤γ<0.50.2\leq\gamma<0.5 is small; 0.5≤γ<0.80.5\leq\gamma<0.8 is medium; γ≥0.8\gamma\geq 0.8 is large.

Large gains from fine-tuning are not expected given the limited training budget (at most 80 epochs with early stopping). Nevertheless, the critical-difference diagram in Figure 3 shows that fine-tuning is effective: the top fine-tuned variants form a cluster that is statistically significantly better than non-pretrained baselines such as xgb_vector and xgblss_Gaussian. For example, finetune_tabiclv2 improves mean CRPS rank from 12.00 (unfine-tuned tabiclv2) to 9.44, moving it into the leading cluster alongside fine-tuned TabPFN variants. TabICLv2 was fine-tuned with the CRPS objective, so it improves on CRPS but not on the log score, consistent with the expectation that fine-tuning shifts a model’s inductive bias toward the optimized scoring rule. TabPFNv2.6 achieves strong R2R^{2} but ranks lower on CRPS and other probabilistic metrics. Conversely, CatBoost improves substantially under CRLS relative to CRPS (see Table 4 and Table 5). Together, these results illustrate ScoringBench’s central message: the choice of metric is not a technicality but determines which model is selected for deployment.

We refer the reader to the live leaderboard at https://scoringbench.com/ for all other metrics (also diagnostic metrics like coverage and sharpness).

While the importance of aligning the scoring rule used for training with application-specific utility is well-established among leading statisticians — most notably popularized by Gneiting and Raftery (2007); Gneiting and Ranjan (2011); Gneiting (2011) and colleagues — its practical implementation in terms of optimal score estimation remains frequently overlooked in modern data science workflows.

In general, we observe—as expected from (Landsgesell and Knoll, 2026)—that the ranking of models depends on the specific scoring rule used to penalize errors (or the chosen scoring function for point estimates (Gneiting, 2011)). This can also be seen by comparing the different leaderboards Table 1, Table 4 and Table 5, see e.g. the entries for TabPFNv2.6.

We also observe that conformal methods like CREPES, when coupled with XGBoost, CatBoost, or TabICLv2, can achieve excellent nominal coverage (see Table 7). However, this coverage benefit comes at a cost: applying CREPES to TabICLv2 degrades performance on the scoring rules TabICLv2 was optimized for. We observe that while coverage improves, the interval score and other proper scoring rules detoriate (see Table 6).

This tradeoff reflects a fundamental distinction between two different evaluation objectives. Conformal methods optimize for agreement with nominal coverage, while proper scoring rules reward both calibration and sharpness simultaneously (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007). Since TabICLv2 is trained on CRPS, wrapping it with a coverage-focused method compromises the distributional quality it was designed to achieve.

For high-risk applications, the choice of evaluation metric should directly reflect the asymmetric costs of different error types (Gneiting, 2011). In weather forecasting, for instance, events more extreme than usual may imply greater damage; consequently, a weighted CRPS is recommended (Gneiting and Ranjan, 2011). Similar logic applies to financial risk management or structural health monitoring (an error that underestimates the stress on a bridge is catastrophic, whereas an overestimation merely leads to conservative maintenance schedules).

5 Conclusion

ScoringBench is an open, extensible benchmark that closes the evaluation gap between the full predictive distributions produced by tabular foundation models and the point estimates measured by prevailing benchmarks. By reporting a comprehensive suite of proper scoring rules alongside standard metrics, ScoringBench enables a more faithful assessment of model quality, especially for applications where the cost of errors is asymmetric.

Empirically, we find three central points. First, model rankings depend strongly on the chosen scoring rule: point-estimate metrics (e.g., R2R^{2}, RMSE) can paint a substantially different picture than proper scoring rules that evaluate full predictive distributions. Second, fine-tuning with alternative scoring rules typically produces small effect sizes (Akinshin’s γ\gamma often in the negligible range) but yields consistent directional shifts across datasets and metrics. Third, pretrained in-context models achieve substantial improvements over gradient-boosted baselines on probabilistic metrics, indicating genuine recent progress in distributional regression.

We therefore recommend that benchmarks include a diverse suite of proper scoring rules and present both rank-based and magnitude-aware summaries. For high-risk applications, practitioners should select (Gneiting, 2011) or design (Merkle and Steyvers, 2013; Oesterheld and Conitzer, 2020) scoring rules that encode domain-specific utility — for instance, weighted CRPS for settings where tail errors are disproportionately costly.

The choice of scoring rule extends beyond regression and directly impacts the training and calibration of modern large-scale classification models. We see ScoringBench as a living resource and welcome community contributions of new datasets, models, and scoring rules via pull request. The code and contribution guide are available at https://github.com/jonaslandsgesell/ScoringBench, the live leaderboard can be found at https://scoringbench.com/.

Appendix A Scoring Rules and Diagnostic Metrics

A.1 Scoring rules

This appendix collects concise definitions of the scoring rules and diagnostic metrics used in ScoringBench. Full implementation notes are available in the repository.

Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS).

For predictive Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) FF and observation yy:

CRPS⁡(F,y)=∫−∞∞(F⁡(x)−𝟏x≥y)2​𝑑x.\mathrm{CRPS}(F,y)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\bigl(F(x)-\mathbf{1}_{x\geq y}\bigr)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x.
Continuous Ranked Logarithmic Score (CRLS).

Following Juutilainen et al. [2012]:

CRLS(F,y)=−∫−∞∞log|F(x)+𝟏{y≤x}−1|dx.\mathrm{CRLS}(F,y)=-\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\log\bigl|F(x)+\mathbf{1}\{y\leq x\}-1\bigr|\,\mathrm{d}x.
Log Score.

If ff is the predictive density of FF:

LogS⁡(F,y)=−log⁡f⁡(y).\mathrm{LogS}(F,y)=-\log f(y).
Density Power Divergence (DPD) scoring rule.

The DPD scoring rule for a predictive density ff is given by Ghosh and Basu [2013]:

Sβ​(f,y)=∫−∞∞f​(t)1+β​𝑑t−(1+1β)​f​(y)β,β>0.S_{\beta}(f,y)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(t)^{1+\beta}\,\mathrm{d}t-\left(1+\frac{1}{\beta}\right)f(y)^{\beta},\qquad\beta>0.

In the limiting case β→0\beta\to 0 this recovers the (negative) log score up to an additive constant:

S0​(f,y)=−log⁡f⁡(y)+const.S_{0}(f,y)=-\log f(y)+\text{const.}

Note for β=1\beta=1 this corresponds to the CDE loss, which is a continuous generalization of the Brier score.

Interval Score

The Interval Score (IS) [Gneiting and Raftery, 2007] evaluates the (1−α)(1{-}\alpha) central prediction interval:

Sα(F,y)=(u−l)+2α(l−y)𝕀{y<l}+2α(y−u)𝕀{y>u},\displaystyle S_{\alpha}(F,y)=(u-l)+\frac{2}{\alpha}(l-y)\mathbb{I}\{y<l\}+\frac{2}{\alpha}(y-u)\mathbb{I}\{y>u\}, (1)

where [l,u][l,u] are the α/2\alpha/2 and 1−α/21{-}\alpha/2 quantiles of the predicted cdf FF.

Quantile Weighted CRPS (wCRPS).

The weighted CRPS can be written as an integral of the pinball loss ρα\rho_{\alpha} over quantile levels α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1]. Using a weight function w⁡(α)w(\alpha) to emphasise regions of interest, a convenient representation is

LwCRPS​(F,y)=2​∫01w⁡(α)​ρα​(y−F−1​(α))​𝑑α,L_{\mathrm{wCRPS}}(F,y)=2\int_{0}^{1}w(\alpha)\,\rho_{\alpha}\bigl(y-F^{-1}(\alpha)\bigr)\,d\alpha,

where the pinball loss is defined by

ρα(u)=(α−𝟏{u<0})u.\rho_{\alpha}(u)=(\alpha-\mathbf{1}\{u<0\})\,u.
The CDE Loss as Continuous Brier Score

The Conditional Density Estimation (CDE) loss (sometimes quadratic score) Rudemo [1982], Izbicki and Lee [2016] generalises the Brier Score Gneiting and Raftery [2007] to continuous outcomes by minimising the L2L^{2} distance between the true density ff and an estimator f^\hat{f}:

L⁡(f,f^)=∫(f⁡(z)−f^​(z))2​𝑑z.L(f,\hat{f})=\int\bigl(f(z)-\hat{f}(z)\bigr)^{2}\,dz.

Dropping the estimator-independent term ∫f2​(z)​𝑑z\int f^{2}(z)\,dz yields the modified CDE loss functional used for estimation:

ℒCDE​(f^,y)=∫f^2​(z)​𝑑z−2​f^​(y).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDE}}(\hat{f},y)=\int\hat{f}^{2}(z)\,dz-2\,\hat{f}(y).

This expression is directly analogous to the discrete Brier loss ∑kpk2−2​py\sum_{k}p_{k}^{2}-2p_{y}, where the integral of the squared density replaces the sum of squared probabilities and the density value at the observation replaces the “hit” probability. Importantly, numerical stability of ℒCDE\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDE}} depends on well-defined supports and strictly monotonic bin boundaries (for example, sorted quantiles in discretised estimators). Violating monotonicity can lead to divergent terms (e.g., from 1/wk1/w_{k}); enforcing sorted quantiles avoids these issues. Because ℒCDE\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDE}} is strictly proper, it incentivises calibrated predictive densities.

A.2 Diagnostic Metrics

Sharpness.

Sharpness measures the concentration of the predictive distribution. Following Tran et al. [2020] we compute sharpness from the model’s estimated predictive CDFs F^n\widehat{F}_{n} for each test point nn as the average predicted standard deviation:

Sharp⁡(F^)=1N​∑n=1Nvar⁡(F^n)=1N​∑n=1N𝔼F^n​[X2]−(𝔼F^n​[X])2.\displaystyle\mathrm{Sharp}(\widehat{F})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sqrt{\mathrm{var}(\widehat{F}_{n})}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{\widehat{F}_{n}}[X^{2}]-\bigl(\mathbb{E}_{\widehat{F}_{n}}[X]\bigr)^{2}}.

Here, F^n\widehat{F}_{n} denotes the model’s estimated predictive CDF for test sample nn, and we write X∼F^nX\sim\widehat{F}_{n}. Define σn=var⁡(F^n)\sigma_{n}=\sqrt{\mathrm{var}(\widehat{F}_{n})} and the mean predicted uncertainty σ¯=1N​∑n=1Nσn\bar{\sigma}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sigma_{n}. Sharpness is not a proper scoring rule; it should be considered jointly with other scoring rules. A well-calibrated model with low sharpness (small predicted standard deviations) provides more actionable uncertainty estimates than one that is calibrated but diffuse [Tran et al., 2020].

Dispersion.

Dispersion measures heterogeneity in the model’s predicted uncertainties across the test set. Using the notation above, let σn=var⁡(F^n)\sigma_{n}=\sqrt{\mathrm{var}(\widehat{F}_{n})} be the predicted standard deviation for sample nn. Then dispersion is the cross-sample standard deviation of these predicted uncertainties:

Disp⁡(F^)=1N−1​∑n=1N(σn−σ¯)2,\displaystyle\mathrm{Disp}(\widehat{F})=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{n=1}^{N}(\sigma_{n}-\bar{\sigma})^{2}},

where σ¯=1N​∑n=1Nσn\bar{\sigma}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sigma_{n}. Dispersion is not a proper scoring rule; it answers the question “how much does the model’s confidence vary across samples?”. A low-dispersion model assigns similar uncertainty estimates to all instances, while a high-dispersion model distinguishes some instances as more predictable than others. Dispersion complements sharpness: two models with the same average sharpness may differ substantially in dispersion.

Higher dispersion is favorable only when true underlying errors are heteroscedastic (i.e., when prediction difficulty genuinely varies across samples). If errors are homoscedastic, a model with high dispersion wastes capacity on spurious confidence variation. We report dispersion alongside sharpness and other metrics for completeness, but treat it as a secondary diagnostic tool (not a primary optimization target) that is only meaningful for datasets with heteroscedastic errors.

Coverage.

For a nominal (1−α)(1-\alpha) prediction interval [l,u][l,u] extracted from the predictive CDF, empirical coverage is the fraction of test points falling inside the interval:

Cov1−α=1n​∑i=1n𝟏li≤yi≤ui.\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}_{1-\alpha}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}_{l_{i}\leq y_{i}\leq u_{i}}.

Here, for the i-th test sample, [li,ui][l_{i},u_{i}] denotes the nominal (1−α)(1-\alpha) predictive interval (lower and upper bounds) extracted from the model’s predictive CDF for that sample, and yiy_{i} is the observed realization of the target. We report coverage at the 90% level (Cov90\mathrm{Cov}_{90}, target 0.90) and the 95% level (Cov95\mathrm{Cov}_{95}, target 0.95). Concretely, for Cov90\mathrm{Cov}_{90} we set α=0.10\alpha=0.10 (nominal level 1−α=0.901-\alpha=0.90) and for Cov95\mathrm{Cov}_{95} we set α=0.05\alpha=0.05 (nominal level 1−α=0.951-\alpha=0.95); α\alpha denotes the total tail probability excluded from a central (1−α)(1-\alpha) interval [li,ui][l_{i},u_{i}]. A well-calibrated model achieves coverage close to the nominal level; the interval score (IS) jointly penalizes over-wide intervals and coverage shortfalls.

Appendix B Benchmark Datasets

We draw candidate datasets from four complementary public repositories (Section B.1), apply a multi-level deduplication procedure to remove redundant entries (Section B.2.1), and filter the remaining candidates to retain only well-formed regression tasks (Section B.2.2). All datasets are available through public APIs (OpenML, PMLB GitHub, KEEL) or direct download URLs without requiring authentication, ensuring full reproducibility. Our guiding principles follow recent calls for higher-quality tabular benchmarks [Erickson et al., 2025, Grinsztajn et al., 2022]: we prioritize diversity across domains and feature dimensionalities, favour datasets derived from genuine data-collection processes, and deduplicate aggressively to avoid inflating the effective benchmark size with near-identical tasks.

B.1 Data Sources

Candidate datasets are drawn from four complementary repositories:

  1. 1.

    OpenML benchmark suites. We include three curated regression suites hosted on OpenML [Vanschoren et al., 2014]:

    • •

      Suite 297 (OpenML-CTR23): a community-curated tabular regression benchmark [Fischer et al., 2023];

    • •

      Suite 299: an additional OpenML regression collection;

    • •

      Suite 269: an OpenML regression collection collating further community-vetted datasets.

    These suites are fetched programmatically via the OpenML Python API and serve as the base layer of our collection.

  2. 2.

    PMLB (Penn Machine Learning Benchmarks). Regression datasets from PMLB [Olson et al., 2017], distributed as compressed TSV files on GitHub. PMLB provides a standardised, version-controlled archive of datasets widely used in AutoML research.

  3. 3.

    KEEL repository. Regression datasets from the KEEL data-mining repository [Derrac et al., 2015], distributed as zipped .dat files. KEEL datasets add coverage of domains less represented in OpenML and PMLB, such as financial time series and energy consumption.

  4. 4.

    TALENT / OpenML verified regression datasets. Additional OpenML datasets drawn from the TALENT benchmark [Liu et al., 2025] and independently verified as regression tasks. This set expands domain coverage to areas including real estate, book reviews, sensor fusion, and sports analytics.

B.2 Dataset construction and filtering

B.2.1 Deduplication Procedure

A central challenge in multi-source dataset aggregation is that the same underlying data frequently appears under different names, numeric identifiers, or preprocessing variants. To avoid having highly correlated (identical) datasets, we apply a four-level deduplication strategy:

  1. 1.

    Exact normalised match. Dataset names are normalised by lowercasing, stripping leading numeric prefixes (e.g., 197_cpu_act →\to cpuact), removing separators and special characters, and collapsing repeated characters. Datasets whose normalised names are identical are treated as duplicates.

  2. 2.

    Substring match. For names longer than three characters, we check whether either normalised name is a substring of the other. This catches common patterns such as houses matching californiahousing.

  3. 3.

    Fuzzy match. We compute a pairwise similarity ratio (via Python’s SequenceMatcher) and flag pairs with ≥85%\geq 85\,\% similarity as duplicates.

  4. 4.

    Explicit deduplication keys. Many datasets are annotated with known aliases (e.g., cpu_act ↔\leftrightarrow cpuact). All checks above are re-applied against these keys.

When a duplicate is detected, we only retain one version and discarding the others, using the (arbitrary) precedence order (OpenML >> PMLB >> KEEL >> scikit-learn).

B.2.2 Validation Filters

After deduplication, every candidate dataset is downloaded and subjected to the following checks:

  • •

    Binary-classification removal. Only datasets with a continuous (or at least multi-valued ordinal) target are retained. Datasets whose target variable contains exactly two unique non-missing values are excluded, as they represent binary classification rather than regression problems. This filter is applied because several OpenML suites and PMLB mix classification and regression tasks under a common umbrella.

  • •

    Target integrity. We favour datasets derived from genuine data-collection processes. Purely synthetic or deterministic-function datasets are included only when they appear in established regression benchmark suites and provide useful diversity in feature–target relationships. We exclude datasets which have non-tabular modalities (images, raw text, audio) and only accept datasets with pure tabular representation. Rows with missing or non-numeric target values are removed. If the target column is stored as a string or categorical type, we convert it to numeric and drop any rows where conversion fails.

B.3 Preprocessing

All datasets undergo lightweight, uniform preprocessing to ensure compatibility with all benchmark models:

  • •

    Missing numeric features are imputed with the column median.

  • •

    Missing categorical features are imputed with the most frequent category.

  • •

    Categorical columns are label-encoded into integer values.

  • •

    No feature scaling or normalisation is applied at the benchmark level; individual model wrappers are free to apply their own transformations internally.

We note that preprocessing choices—imputation strategies, categorical encoding, and any scaling—act as modelling hyperparameters that can materially affect downstream performance. Different model families benefit from different strategies, and several modern algorithms support native handling of missing values. In a future release we will provide an alternative benchmark configuration that omits benchmark-level imputation, enabling direct comparison of methods that handle missing values natively.

B.4 Final dataset overview

Table 2 enumerates the datasets in ScoringBench after deduplication and validation.

The final number of datasets used in any given experiment depends on which candidates survive all deduplication and validation steps. The authoritative, machine-readable dataset list is exported as datasets.json at the start of every benchmark run. If any datasets fails on too many models (e.g., due to memory errors), it is automatically removed from the final results to prevent skewing the analysis.

Appendix C Experimental protocol

C.1 Cross-Validation Protocol

Each dataset is evaluated using stratified KK-fold cross-validation (CV) with K=5K=5 folds and a fixed random seed (seed = 42) for reproducibility. The number of CV repeats defaults to 1 but can be increased with --n_repeats_cv to obtain tighter confidence estimates.

C.2 Downsampling after CV split

To ensure computational feasibility and to prevent very large datasets from dominating the benchmark, each cross-validation repeat draws a random subsample of at most Nmax=3000=2,400​(train)+600​(test)N_{\max}=3000=2{,}400\text{(train)}+600\text{(test)} observations (configurable via --sample_size). Subsampling is performed inside the CV loop so that each repeat sees a different random subset, improving robustness through less correlation in the folds. Future versions of the benchmark may study sample efficiency by measuring how model performance scales with training-set size; this requires evaluating multiple training-sample sizes per dataset. As an ablation, we also evaluate the effect of capping the total dataset size (training plus test) at 1000 and 2000 observations, see Appendix E.

C.3 Evaluation

For each CV split and each model, we compute the fold-averaged score s¯m,d,p\bar{s}_{m,d,p} on held out data (from the CV split) for each metric pp on dataset dd.

Appendix D Ranking Approaches

D.1 Demšar–autorank approach (Autorank)

Autorank strictly follows the Demšar protocol [Demšar, 2006] and relies on the implementation in the autorank library [Herbold, 2020]. This approach discards score magnitudes and operates solely on ordinal ranks. Let m∈{1,…,M}m\in\{1,\dots,M\} denote a model, d∈{1,…,D}d\in\{1,\dots,D\} a dataset, and pp a specific performance metric. The procedure is as follows [Demšar, 2006]:

  • •

    For each dataset dd and metric pp, the models mm are ranked based on their fold-averaged scores s¯m,d,p\bar{s}_{m,d,p}. The best-performing model receives rank 1, the second-best rank 2, and so on. This transforms the data into the shape (model ​m,dataset ​d,rank ​rm,d,p)(\text{model }m,\;\text{dataset }d,\;\text{rank }r_{m,d,p}).33 3 In contrast to the scoring rules, minimizing coverage is not desirable but we need to judge goodness by its agreement with the nominal level. For ranking we, therefore, have to transform coverage and we rank according to |Cov1−α−(1−α)||\mathrm{Cov}_{1-\alpha}-(1-\alpha)| instead of Cov1−α\mathrm{Cov}_{1-\alpha}.

  • •

    Next, the mean rank r¯m,p\bar{r}_{m,p} for each model mm on metric pp is computed by averaging across all DD datasets, yielding the mean rank

    r¯m,p=1D​∑d=1Drm,d,p\displaystyle\bar{r}_{m,p}=\frac{1}{D}\sum_{d=1}^{D}r_{m,d,p} (2)
  • •

    The non-parametric Friedman test then evaluates whether these mean ranks r¯m,p\bar{r}_{m,p} differ significantly across the MM models for a given metric pp.

  • •

    If the omnibus Friedman test is significant at level α=0.05\alpha=0.05, the post-hoc Nemenyi test [Nemenyi, 1963] identifies which specific pairs of models differ. The Nemenyi test defines a critical difference (CD) threshold [Demšar, 2006]:

    CD=qα​M⁡(M+1)6​D,\displaystyle\mathrm{CD}=q_{\alpha}\sqrt{\frac{M(M+1)}{6D}}\,, (3)

    where qαq_{\alpha} is the critical value from the studentised range distribution divided by 2\sqrt{2}.

  • •

    Two models are considered statistically significantly different if the absolute difference between their mean ranks exceeds the value CD\mathrm{CD} computed in Eq. (3).

Autorank automatically selects appropriate summary statistics, confidence-interval methods, and effect-size measures for reporting. Furthermore, it automatically creates critical difference (CD) diagrams like the one in Figure 3.

To partially mitigate the loss of magnitude information inherent in rank-based tests, autorank augments each model’s evaluation with Akinshin’s γ\gamma, a non-parametric effect size analogous to Cohen’s dd. Akinshin’s γ\gamma quantifies the standardized difference between two score distributions without parametric assumptions; we report it computed against the top-ranked model.

D.2 Standardised magnitude-based ranking (z-score ranking)

The second approach retains performance magnitude information by standardising the fold-averaged scores s¯m,d,p\bar{s}_{m,d,p} (see Eq. (4)) within each dataset before aggregating them. Starting with the data in the shape (model ​m,dataset ​d,mean score ​s¯m,d,p)(\text{model }m,\;\text{dataset }d,\;\text{mean score }\bar{s}_{m,d,p}), we compute a zz-score to normalize for dataset difficulty:

zm,d,p=s¯m,d,p−μd,pσd,p+ϵ,z_{m,d,p}\;=\;\frac{\bar{s}_{m,d,p}-\mu_{d,p}}{\sigma_{d,p}+\epsilon}\,, (4)

where the dataset- and metric-specific mean μd,p\mu_{d,p} and standard deviation σd,p\sigma_{d,p} are defined across the MM models as:

μd,p=1M​∑m=1Ms¯m,d,p,σd,p=1M−1​∑m=1M(s¯m,d,p−μd,p)2.\displaystyle\mu_{d,p}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\bar{s}_{m,d,p}\,,\qquad\sigma_{d,p}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\bigl(\bar{s}_{m,d,p}-\mu_{d,p}\bigr)^{2}}\,.

Here, ϵ=10−9\epsilon=10^{-9} prevents division by zero, and σd,p\sigma_{d,p} is estimated with M−1M-1 degrees of freedom. This standardisation transforms the data into the shape:

(model ​m,dataset ​d,z​-score ​zm,d,p),\displaystyle(\text{model }m,\penalty\ \text{dataset }d,\penalty\ z\text{-score }z_{m,d,p})\,,

expressing each model’s performance in units of the cross-model standard deviation on dataset dd. Crucially, this standardisation centers and scales scores within each dataset (subtracting the dataset mean and dividing by the cross-model standard deviation), removing dataset-specific location and scale so that resulting zm,d,pz_{m,d,p} values reflect relative performance across models independent of metric scale or dataset difficulty.

For metrics pp where lower values indicate better performance, the sign of zm,d,pz_{m,d,p} is negated so that higher standardised scores uniformly represent superior performance (e.g. for CRPS, lower is better, so we use −zm,d,p-z_{m,d,p} instead of zm,d,pz_{m,d,p}). The final aggregated ranking score for model mm on metric pp is obtained by averaging its standardised zz-scores across all DD datasets:

z¯m,p=1D​∑d=1Dzm,d,p.\displaystyle\bar{z}_{m,p}\;=\;\frac{1}{D}\sum_{d=1}^{D}z_{m,d,p}\,.

Models are then ranked in descending order based on z¯m,p\bar{z}_{m,p}.

We compare both ranking approaches in Figure 4. The figure shows, for every model, how many times it was placed Top1 and how many times it was placed in the Top3 under each approach. Similar Top1 and Top3 counts across the two methods indicate stability — the same models are repeatedly identified as winners and leaders; large differences imply the ranking choice materially changes which models are considered top performers. Additionally, a Pearson correlation between the two rank vectors is computed to quantify their agreement, see Section D.3.

D.3 Ranking stability between both ranking approaches

To assess whether our conclusions depend on the ranking method, we compare Autorank and z-score rankings across all metrics. For each metric, we record which model is ranked first and which models appear in the top three under each method (Figure 4).

The two approaches largely agree: the Pearson correlation between their rank vectors has a mean of 0.900.90 and a median of 0.970.97 across metrics (Table 3), meaning both methods typically identify the same top-performing models. The main outlier is cde_loss (r=0.655r=0.655), where the ranking method materially affects which models appear at the top. Given this overall agreement, reporting only the Autorank-based leaderboards in the main text is justified; both rankings for every metric are available on the live leaderboard at https://scoringbench.com/.

D.4 Additional ranking results

In the main text, the CRPS-based leaderboard was reported in Table 1. Here we report as well the autorank R2R^{2}-based leaderboard as well as a autorank CRLS-based leaderboard, see Table 4 and Table 5 (due to high correlation between both ranking methods, we report only the autorank-based leaderboards in the main text; the z-score-based leaderboards are available in the online leaderboard https://scoringbench.example.com).

Table 4 gives Autorank rankings for R2R^{2}. Columns report mean R2R^{2} and the mean rank across datasets.

Appendix E Ablation study with respect to data set size

To investigate if our ranking results are robust to the choice of dataset size, we perform an ablation study where we re-run the benchmark on all datasets but with a reduced capped dataset size of 1000, 2000, 3000 and 8000 samples (test + train size). The results are shown in Figure 5.

We observe some minor variation across metrics and models; this is expected because different scoring rules can have different finite-sample efficiencies and may converge at different speeds during finetuning, which can affect rankings at smaller sample sizes [Waghmare and Ziegel, 2025].

Let ℳa,b(p)\mathcal{M}_{a,b}^{(p)} be the set of models common to sample-size outputs (folders) aa and bb for metric pp, where na,b(p)=|ℳa,b(p)|n_{a,b}^{(p)}=|\mathcal{M}_{a,b}^{(p)}|. For each model i∈ℳa,b(p)i\in\mathcal{M}_{a,b}^{(p)}, let ri(a,p)r^{(a,p)}_{i} and ri(b,p)r^{(b,p)}_{i} be its ranks in folders aa and bb for metric pp. The Spearman rank correlation ρa,b(p)\rho^{(p)}_{a,b} is defined as:

ρa,b(p)=∑i=1na,b(p)(ri(a,p)−r¯(a,p))​(ri(b,p)−r¯(b,p))∑i=1na,b(p)(ri(a,p)−r¯(a,p))2​∑i=1na,b(p)(ri(b,p)−r¯(b,p))2\rho^{(p)}_{a,b}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n_{a,b}^{(p)}}\left(r^{(a,p)}_{i}-\bar{r}^{(a,p)}\right)\left(r^{(b,p)}_{i}-\bar{r}^{(b,p)}\right)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n_{a,b}^{(p)}}\left(r^{(a,p)}_{i}-\bar{r}^{(a,p)}\right)^{2}}\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n_{a,b}^{(p)}}\left(r^{(b,p)}_{i}-\bar{r}^{(b,p)}\right)^{2}}}

where r¯(a,p)\bar{r}^{(a,p)} and r¯(b,p)\bar{r}^{(b,p)} are the mean ranks. Ties are handled by assigning average ranks.

Appendix F Workflow for contributing to the benchmark

In order to facilitate contributions to our benchmark from other researchers, we briefly elaborate on the workflow to do so.

  1. 1.

    git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/jonaslandsgesell/ScoringBench.git, make sure to have git-lfs installed.

  2. 2.

    Add your custom wrapper with a unique name to the folder scoringbench/wrapper/ following the template of existing wrappers. Ensure it adheres to the expected interface for seamless integration.

  3. 3.

    Run the benchmarking via python run_bench_regression.py (or parallelize via slurm with sbatch array=0103 run_benchmark.sbatch)

  4. 4.

    Run the ranking method by executing python autorank_leaderboard.py which will evaluate both Autorank and z-score ranking and generate the leaderboard outputs.

  5. 5.

    Commit your model parquet file (documenting each run) and the updated leaderboard CSVs in /output/figures/leaderboard/. Since the output repository is separate from the main repository, push to both. This serves as a public ledger and allows traceability.

  6. 6.

    Create a pull request to the ScoringBench repository for review; contributions that meet standards will be merged.

  7. 7.

    Upon merge, https://scoringbench.com/ will automatically display the updated leaderboard and data is archived in the git lfs repository for reproducibility.
